title: Beha'alotcha: we remember the fish (Numbers 11:4–6)
hookLine: the people crave Egypt's fish and cucumbers, forgetting the whip

cards: Someone runs into an ex at a party, and for one dangerous second remembers only the good parts. The road trip. The inside joke.
The way they made coffee. Somehow the months of feeling small have gone blurry. Or it's an old job they hated, and now they catch themselves saying, the people were great, though.
Memory is a generous editor: it keeps the flavor and cuts the cost. The Israelites, out of slavery and eating manna in the desert, do exactly this, and the Torah quotes their grocery list.

teach.b: Numbers eleven. The camp starts to crave.

First the mixed crowd that came out of Egypt with them, then everyone, weeping in their tent doorways: "We remember the fish, which we were wont to eat in Egypt for nought; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlic".
Now, they say, our throats are dry, and there's nothing but this manna. You can almost smell the list. But look at two words: for nought.
Free. The fish in Egypt were free? The rabbis didn't buy it.
The Sifrei, and Rashi after it, ask: these people weren't even given straw for free to make their bricks. Who was handing them free fish?

No, the rabbis say, free meant free of commandments, free of responsibility. In Egypt nobody asked anything of them but labor, and nobody expected them to choose. That's a kind of ease, and it's real.

teach.h: THE LIST LEAVES OUT THE WHIP.
teach.b: And notice what the list leaves out. No whip. No quota of bricks.
No baby boys thrown into the river. The craving doesn't lie about the cucumbers; it just forgets everything around them. The Torah doesn't mock them for missing food.
Missing things is human. It just puts their own words on the record, so anyone reading later can hear what nostalgia does.

how: The people's craving for Egypt's food in Numbers 11 is read in Beha'alotcha each summer; Jewish teachers often use Rashi's reading of "for nought" to talk about how the memory of slavery can be softened into longing.

o: the manna that fell each morning in the desert
the complaint the people made in the camp
when you raise up: the portion of the lamps

games.q: what the craving remembers — tap the pairs.

s: the rabbis took the free fish in Egypt at face value
they asked how slaves denied free straw got free fish.
the craving began with the mixed crowd and spread to everyone
Numbers 11:4: then the children of Israel wept too.
the Torah mocks the people for missing food
it records their words; missing things is human.

games.q: you're in the desert, eating manna. someone sighs: remember the free fish in Egypt? how do the rabbis answer that "free"?
o: Egypt really did feed its slaves well.
free meant free of commandments, not free of cost.
the fish were a gift from Pharaoh.
games.why: the Sifrei and Rashi: they weren't even given straw for free. "for nought" means free of the commandments: an easy kind of unfreedom.

practice: Let one old place come back to you, a job, a relationship, a city, a habit you quit, and notice the first memories that arrive: probably the cucumbers.
Then gently ask for the rest of the picture, what it cost you to be there and what you left for a reason. You don't have to hate the place; just hold the flavor and the cost together.

wordCard.voice: Beha'alotcha, the portion of the lamps, and of the night the people wept for Egypt's fish and forgot its whip.

orig.note: Hebrew: for nothing, free. the word the people use for Egypt's fish.

carryVoice: Your line: Egypt wasn't free. Memory kept the cucumbers and dropped the whip. See you tomorrow.
